newsitem.title: FRANCE: French, German finance officials in EMU talks.
newsitem.headline: French, German finance officials in EMU talks.

text.p: France and Germany, the leaders in the drive to European monetary union, were expected on Wednesday to reaffirm their determination to launch a single currency on time in January 1999.

French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis, German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, and French and German central bank heads Jean-Claude Trichet and Hans Tietmeyer were holding talks here on the single currency and the economic outlook.
Arthuis told reporters he would reiterate his belief that Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) would start on time.
"I will reaffirm my conviction that we will be there on January 1, 1999," he said as he arrived for the talks in the central French town of Lyon.
"We must all prepare to be there on January 1, 1999. To consider that we do not respect this timetable is to give up on it in advance," he said in an interview with local Lyon newspaper Le Progres.
The meeting, part of a regular series between the finance ministers and central bankers of Europe's two biggest economies, takes place amid resurgent speculation about a delay to EMU.
This has been fuelled by worries that Germany may be unable to cut its budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product this year in line with Maastricht treaty requirements.

But Waigel told Reuters that Germany was in a position to keep its deficit below the three percent product this year, the key year for deciding which countries qualify to join a single currency when it is first launched in 1999.
He also said that both Germany and France were in a good position to achieve 2.5 percent economic growth this year.
Arthuis told Le Progres he was confident Germany would meet Maastricht treaty requirements.

"There are indeed questions in Germany about its ability to respect the (Maastricht) convergence criteria...Nonetheless I do not doubt the ability of the German authorities to take the necessary measures to meet their commitments," he said.
"Moreover, nor do I doubt the ability of other countries in the European Union, and I want as many countries as possible to qualify for the switch to the euro," he added.
Many private economists believe that Germany will overshoot the three percent target, as unemployment, at a postwar record, bites into tax revenues.
Although the Maastricht treaty allows some leeway on deficits and debt, the question is complicated by Italy's insistence that it join the single currency from the start.
Germany is believed to be very reluctant to allow Italy, Spain and Portugal into EMU when it is first launched, fearing this would undermine the credibility of the new currency.
But any overshooting by Bonn on the deficit criterion will make it harder to exclude other countries, like Italy, expected by private economists to fall short of the three percent target.

A French finance ministry official said earlier this week the talks would also touch on France's proposal for a stability council to oversee economic policies in the euro zone and look at international efforts towards reducing taxation anomalies which give some countries an unfair competitive advantage.

The talks had been scheduled to end with a joint news conference at 1145 GMT. However officials said this might be delayed after Waigel arrived around an hour late for the start after flying to the wrong airport.
